subtopic_detail: HEEADSSS assessment - sensitive-topic order and confidentiality
stem:
A 15-year-old girl presents to a metropolitan general practice with her mother for headaches over three months. Her mother speaks for her throughout the introduction. On paper screening the girl endorses "low mood most days" and "trouble at school".

You are the GP registrar. You have 25 minutes, no prior relationship with the family, and you want to complete a psychosocial screen while she is here today.

Her mother is willing to step out but asks that you "tell her anything worrying".

data_table.Setting: GP registrar, 25 minute appointment, first visit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial approach to the psychosocial interview?

options.text: Explain confidentiality limits, ask mother to wait outside, then begin with Home and Education before Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide and Safety
options.rationale: The HEEADSSS framework is deliberately ordered from least to most sensitive so rapport is built on lower-stakes domains before drugs, sexuality and suicide. Confidentiality (and its limits: risk to self, risk to others, abuse) is set out BEFORE any sensitive disclosure so the adolescent can decide what to share. Interviewing without the parent present from adolescence onward is standard AU practice (Source: RACGP - Confidential health care for adolescents and young adults; headspace clinical practice guidelines).
source_refs: RACGP Confidential health care for adolescents and young adults

options.text: Keep her mother in the room so collateral is available and start with drugs and sexual activity while she is willing to talk
options.rationale: Adolescents systematically under-report sensitive content in front of a parent; starting with drugs or sexuality without rapport violates the HEEADSSS ordering and is likely to yield a false-negative screen (Source: headspace clinical practice guidelines).

options.text: Defer psychosocial screening to a dedicated youth mental health service and address only the headache today
options.rationale: The GP is the first-line setting for HEEADSSS in Australia and deferring risks missing self-harm or safety concerns already flagged on paper screening (Source: RACGP).
source_refs: RACGP Confidential health care for adolescents and young adults

options.text: Promise complete confidentiality so she will disclose, then decide later whether to inform her mother
options.rationale: Unqualified confidentiality is never appropriate; risk to self, risk to others and mandatory child-protection reporting are non-negotiable exceptions that must be named upfront (Source: RACGP).
source_refs: RACGP Confidential health care for adolescents and young adults

options.text: Ask her mother to summarise the girl's mood, substance use and any sexual activity before speaking with her alone
options.rationale: Parental report substitutes for the adolescent's own account and normalises the parent as the primary informant on sensitive domains; the interview should start with the adolescent (Source: headspace).

explanation.summary: HEEADSSS is ordered from least to most sensitive (Home, Education, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide, Safety) with confidentiality and its limits set out before the sensitive domains, and the adolescent seen alone.
key_points: See adolescents alone from about 12-13 onwards, offering to invite family in later
State confidentiality limits upfront: risk to self, risk to others, mandatory reporting
Order matters - rapport before drugs, sexuality, suicide
GP is the AU first-line setting; do not defer to specialist services for initial screen
explanation.pearls: The additional S at the end (Safety - including online and cyberbullying) is now standard AU practice.

sources.label: RACGP Confidential health care for adolescents and young adults

subtopic_detail: Gillick / mature-minor consent and confidentiality limits
stem:
A 15-year-old boy attends a NSW community youth clinic alone and requests SSRI treatment for depression that he has been discussing with his school counsellor for six months. He describes anhedonia, poor sleep and impaired school performance, and denies suicidal ideation, hallucinations, substance use or coercion. He answers questions about the medication rationale, expected onset, common side effects, activation risk and the plan for parental involvement in a way that shows he understands and is weighing them.

He explicitly asks that his parents not be told. His parents are separated and he lives with his mother. There are no child-protection concerns.

You are the paediatric registrar covering the clinic.

data_table.Assessment: No suicidal ideation, no psychosis, no substance use, no coercion
data_table.Capacity screen: Understands, retains, weighs and communicates a choice about SSRI

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response to his request for treatment?

options.text: Commence fluoxetine and document Gillick-competent consent, offering (not requiring) parental involvement and recording his reasons for confidentiality
options.rationale: A mature minor who understands the nature, purpose and reasonably foreseeable consequences of the proposed treatment may consent independently under the Gillick / mature-minor principle adopted by AU courts. Depression care in an adolescent is within that scope. Parental involvement is offered and encouraged but is not a legal prerequisite when the young person has capacity and there is no safeguarding concern (Source: RACGP Confidential health care for adolescents and young adults; RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry guidance).
source_refs: RACGP Confidential health care for adolescents and young adults
RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Decline to start any medication until a parent countersigns the consent form
options.rationale: Parental countersignature is not required for a Gillick-competent minor and denying treatment on that basis is inconsistent with AU consent law (Source: RACGP).
source_refs: RACGP Confidential health care for adolescents and young adults

options.text: Contact his mother today to obtain consent because he is under 16 years
options.rationale: The 16-year rule is a threshold above which competence is presumed, not a floor below which competence is impossible; overriding a competent minor breaches confidentiality without justification (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Refer to a Children's Court to authorise treatment given his age
options.rationale: Court authorisation is reserved for special medical procedures (sterilisation, gender-affirming stage 3) or disputed consent where the young person lacks capacity, not routine SSRI initiation in a competent minor (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Prescribe the SSRI on the condition he agrees you will phone his mother the same day
options.rationale: Conditional confidentiality-breach as a price of care is coercive and violates the confidentiality he has explicitly requested and is entitled to as a competent minor (Source: RACGP).
source_refs: RACGP Confidential health care for adolescents and young adults

explanation.summary: A mature minor with capacity may consent to their own mental-health treatment; parental involvement is offered rather than required, provided there are no safeguarding concerns and no legal exception (special medical procedures) applies.
key_points: Gillick / mature-minor test: understands, retains, weighs, communicates
Confidentiality is default; limits are risk-to-self, risk-to-others, mandatory reporting
Age 16 is a presumption threshold, not an absolute cut-off
Special medical procedures (sterilisation, stage-3 gender-affirming) need court oversight when parents disagree
explanation.pearls: Always document the specific reasoning that led to the capacity finding; do not just tick a box.

sources.label: RACGP Confidential health care for adolescents and young adults
RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

subtopic_detail: Youth suicide - highest-risk demographic and means restriction
stem:
You are the RMO in a rural NSW emergency department reviewing a 17-year-old boy after his father brought him in following a text message that read "I can't do this anymore". He describes escalating hopelessness over four weeks after a relationship breakup and school suspension. He denies current intent but says he has thought about "how it would happen" over the past week.

The family lives on a working farm 40 minutes from town. There is a locked gun safe with two rifles used for pest control, and a shed with several boxes of paracetamol and other over-the-counter medications kept for the household.

He is medically well and has no prior mental-health contact.

data_table.Suicidality: Passive ideation four weeks, method rumination one week, no current intent
data_table.Access to means: Locked farm rifles (father holds key); household paracetamol stockpile
data_table.Setting: Rural NSW, 40 minute drive from ED

lead_in: In addition to arranging urgent mental-health review, which is the single most impactful safety-planning action tonight?

options.text: Agree with the father that all firearms and household paracetamol stockpiles will be removed from the home overnight
options.rationale: Means restriction is the single most evidence-based population and individual intervention for youth suicide, and the demographic at highest completed-suicide risk in Australia is young men aged 15-24, particularly in rural areas where firearm access is greater. Restricting BOTH firearms (highest lethality) and paracetamol (highest volume of adolescent overdose) addresses the two dominant AU adolescent-suicide methods (Source: Beyond Blue - Suicide prevention in young men; AIHW Suicide and self-harm monitoring).
source_refs: Beyond Blue youth suicide prevention resources

options.text: Have him sign a written no-suicide contract before discharge home tonight
options.rationale: No-suicide contracts have no evidence of reducing suicide and are not endorsed by current AU or international guidance; they may give false reassurance (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Reassure the father that a locked gun safe is sufficient protection given his son has no current intent
options.rationale: A locked safe in the home does not equal means restriction; keys and combinations are often known or accessible, and impulsive access remains possible during a crisis (Source: Beyond Blue).
source_refs: Beyond Blue youth suicide prevention resources

options.text: Prescribe a two-week supply of an SSRI to be held by the father and reviewed in one month
options.rationale: SSRI initiation without close follow-up in the first 1-2 weeks (activation and paradoxical suicidality risk) is inappropriate for a rural patient 40 minutes from services; assessment and safety planning come first (Source: AMH; headspace).

options.text: Refer to school counsellor follow-up next Monday as the primary safety plan
options.rationale: School counsellor follow-up in three days is not the acute safety action; the immediate priority is removal of lethal means from the home while specialist review is arranged (Source: headspace).

explanation.summary: Rural young men aged 15-24 are Australia's highest-risk demographic for completed suicide; means restriction (firearms and medication stockpiles) is the single most effective intervention alongside urgent specialist review.
key_points: AIHW: highest age-specific suicide rate in males 15-24 is in rural and remote areas
Firearms carry the highest case-fatality; paracetamol is the highest-volume method
Means restriction should extend beyond the individual to the household
No-suicide contracts do not reduce suicide
explanation.pearls: Safety plan should be collaborative, written, and include warning signs, coping strategies, social contacts, professional contacts, and means restriction.

sources.label: Beyond Blue youth suicide prevention resources
RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

subtopic_detail: NSSI vs suicide attempt - differentiation and DBT-A indication
stem:
A 16-year-old girl is reviewed by the youth mental-health registrar after her third presentation in six months for superficial forearm laceration with a razor blade. She describes cutting when "nothing else stops the noise in my head" and reports immediate relief and no intent to die at any of the episodes. Each time she has told a friend afterwards.

She reports chronic emotion dysregulation since age 12, unstable friendships, rapid mood shifts and a sense of emptiness, but no discrete depressive episode. She has no current suicidal plan. She has attended six sessions of supportive counselling with limited progress.

Her parents are engaged and asking what treatment is likely to help.

data_table.Behaviour: Repeated superficial cutting, tension-relief function, no death intent, disclosed to peers
data_table.Traits: Chronic emotion dysregulation, unstable relationships, emptiness since age 12
data_table.Prior treatment: Six sessions supportive counselling, limited progress

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next treatment recommendation?

options.text: Refer for dialectical behaviour therapy for adolescents with concurrent family skills training
options.rationale: The pattern of repetitive non-suicidal self-injury with tension-relief function and pervasive emotion dysregulation from early adolescence is the exact indication for DBT-A, which has the strongest evidence for reducing self-injury and improving emotion regulation in this group; parallel family skills training is a core component (Source: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry; headspace clinical practice guidelines).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Commence an SSRI as first-line treatment for the underlying mood component
options.rationale: There is no discrete depressive episode meeting criteria; SSRIs are not first-line for emotion-dysregulation-driven self-injury and do not reduce repetitive self-harm (Source: AMH; headspace).

options.text: Admit to an adolescent inpatient unit for the duration of skill acquisition
options.rationale: Prolonged admission for chronic non-suicidal self-injury is associated with regression and iatrogenic dependence; brief admission is reserved for acute suicidality (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Prescribe a low-dose quetiapine as required for distress and self-harm urges
options.rationale: As-required sedating antipsychotic for distress lacks evidence, risks metabolic harm and pharmacological coping-avoidance; not recommended for this indication (Source: AMH).

options.text: Continue supportive counselling for a further twelve sessions before escalating care
options.rationale: Six sessions of supportive counselling with limited progress in an adolescent with clear DBT-A indication is a plateau; continuing an ineffective modality delays evidence-based care (Source: headspace).

explanation.summary: Repetitive non-suicidal self-injury with tension-relief function in an adolescent with pervasive emotion dysregulation is the primary indication for DBT-A with a family skills component.
key_points: NSSI: functional (relief) act without death intent
DSM-5 recognises NSSI Disorder distinct from suicidal self-directed violence
DBT-A: individual + skills group + family + phone coaching
Do not equate NSSI with low risk - it is the strongest predictor of future attempt
explanation.pearls: Any NSSI in adolescence increases the odds of a future suicide attempt roughly threefold; separate risk assessment from motive assessment.

sources.label: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

subtopic_detail: Anorexia nervosa - MARSIPAN-AU refeeding start rate
stem:
You are the paediatric medical registrar admitting a 15-year-old girl with anorexia nervosa to the ward. She is 165 cm and 40 kg (BMI 14.7). Estimated oral intake over the past three weeks has been 300-500 kcal per day. Weighing her admission bloods: sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), phosphate 0.82 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), magnesium 0.80 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L. Her supine heart rate is 42 with a postural rise of 18. Temperature is 35.6 degrees Celsius. ECG shows QTc 440 ms.

Her bed is now on cardiac telemetry, thiamine 300 mg IV daily has been charted, and the family are pushing for "a proper meal plan" that will "actually start putting weight back on her".

Her weight has been declining by roughly 500 g per week.

data_table.Vitals: HR 42 supine, postural HR rise 18, temp 35.6 C, QTc 440 ms
data_table.Bloods: Na 138, K 3.6, PO4 0.82, Mg 0.80, corrected Ca 2.32, all within normal limits

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial refeeding prescription?

options.text: Commence oral feeds providing 1400 kcal per day with prophylactic oral phosphate and daily electrolyte monitoring for the first week
options.rationale: ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU guidance for high-risk adolescents advises starting at roughly 1400-1800 kcal/day (about 30-40 kcal/kg for this patient) with prophylactic phosphate and DAILY electrolyte monitoring for the first week. Historic very-low-start regimens (5-10 kcal/kg) are now recognised as under-feeding and prolong medical instability; the risk is over-restriction, not refeeding syndrome, provided phosphate is replaced and monitored (Source: ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU; RCH Melbourne CPG - Eating disorders).

options.text: Commence oral feeds providing 400 kcal per day and advance by 200 kcal every third day
options.rationale: The under-feeding paradigm (5-10 kcal/kg/day starts) has been superseded in AU adolescent practice; it prolongs weight loss and medical instability without preventing refeeding syndrome when phosphate is replaced (Source: ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU).

options.text: Commence oral feeds providing 3000 kcal per day to reverse weight loss rapidly and monitor electrolytes weekly
options.rationale: Starting at 3000 kcal/day exceeds even the aggressive-refeeding upper bound and pairing it with only weekly monitoring risks unrecognised hypophosphataemia (Source: ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU).

options.text: Begin nasogastric feeding at 40 mL per hour of standard formula and withhold oral intake for the first 72 hours
options.rationale: NG is reserved for refusal of oral intake or medical inability to eat; a girl who can eat orally should be commenced on supervised oral refeeding first (Source: ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU).

options.text: Withhold refeeding for 48 hours until phosphate replacement has been given and electrolytes rechecked
options.rationale: Prophylactic phosphate is given ALONGSIDE feeding, not instead of it; delaying feeding worsens catabolism without evidence of benefit (Source: RCH Melbourne CPG - Eating disorders).

explanation.summary: AU MARSIPAN adolescent refeeding starts at around 1400-1800 kcal/day (about 30-40 kcal/kg) with prophylactic phosphate and daily electrolyte monitoring in the first week; very-low-calorie starts are outdated.
key_points: Refeeding syndrome triad: hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia
Thiamine before or with the first meaningful carbohydrate load
Prophylactic oral phosphate 500 mg tds is typical starting dose
Daily bloods for at least 5-7 days
explanation.pearls: The AU shift from the old 5-10 kcal/kg regimen was driven by evidence that under-feeding IS itself a harm.

subtopic_detail: Bulimia nervosa in adolescents - first-line psychotherapy
stem:
A 17-year-old girl presents to the community youth mental health service with a nine-month history of binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting occurring three to four times per week. She is medically stable, BMI 22, has no electrolyte derangement, and her school attendance is preserved. She lives at home with two supportive parents and has no comorbid substance use or self-harm.

She describes intense guilt after binges and preoccupation with body weight, and would like help. Her parents are willing to be involved in whatever treatment is recommended.

She has had no previous mental-health treatment.

data_table.Context: Living at home, engaged supportive parents, no comorbidity

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment recommendation?

options.text: Family-based treatment adapted for adolescent bulimia with parents supporting normalised eating
options.rationale: For adolescents (roughly under 19 years) living with engaged parents, family-based treatment adapted for bulimia (FBT-BN) is the first-line psychological therapy in AU practice, with cognitive behavioural therapy enhanced for adolescents (CBT-E) as the main alternative when family involvement is not feasible or the young person prefers individual work (Source: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry; ANZAED).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Fluoxetine 60 mg daily as the primary standalone intervention
options.rationale: Fluoxetine has evidence in adult bulimia but is not first-line monotherapy in adolescents; where used it is adjunctive to a structured psychological therapy (Source: AMH).

options.text: Weekly supportive counselling with a school psychologist and monthly GP review
options.rationale: Generic supportive counselling has consistently underperformed against structured eating-disorder therapies in adolescents; not first-line (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Admission to a specialist adolescent eating-disorder inpatient program for eight weeks
options.rationale: Bulimia at this severity in a medically stable adolescent is managed in the community; inpatient admission is reserved for medical instability, severe suicidality, or failed community treatment (Source: ANZAED).

options.text: Topiramate as the primary intervention to reduce binge frequency
options.rationale: Topiramate has some adult evidence for binge reduction but is not first-line in adolescents and carries teratogenicity, cognitive slowing and weight-loss concerns unhelpful in this population (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Adolescent bulimia in a young person still living with engaged parents is first-line treated with family-based treatment adapted for bulimia; CBT-E is the main alternative.
key_points: FBT-BN empowers parents to disrupt the binge-purge cycle
CBT-E is the primary individual alternative
Fluoxetine 60 mg is adult second-line, adolescent adjunct only
Medical stability governs setting (community vs inpatient)
explanation.pearls: The Maudsley family-based approach originated in anorexia; the bulimia adaptation is a distinct manualised therapy.

sources.label: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

subtopic_detail: ARFID vs picky eating - differentiating features
stem:
A 13-year-old boy is brought by his mother to a paediatric outpatient clinic because he "only eats about ten foods". He has always been a selective eater but the range has narrowed since primary school. He now refuses all foods with a wet or mixed texture, gags on new foods, and eats predominantly plain pasta, dry crackers and chicken nuggets. He has lost 4 kg over the last six months and has stopped growing along his previously steady centile. His weight has crossed from the 50th to the 15th percentile.

His iron studies show ferritin 12 microg/L (30-300) and haemoglobin 108 g/L (130-170). He is not preoccupied with body shape or weight, denies fear of fatness, and eats freely in front of others when it is a preferred food.

There is no other developmental or medical diagnosis.

data_table.Feeding pattern: About 10 foods; wet/mixed textures refused with gagging
data_table.Growth: 4 kg loss / 6 months; weight 50th to 15th percentile
data_table.Body image: No preoccupation, no fear of fatness

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate diagnosis and management pairing?

options.text: Avoidant restrictive food intake disorder; refer for multidisciplinary eating-disorder assessment and treat iron deficiency
options.rationale: Restrictive intake with sensory-based food avoidance, weight loss and nutritional deficiency in the absence of body-image disturbance meets DSM-5 criteria for avoidant restrictive food intake disorder. Weight drop across two centiles plus iron-deficient anaemia is above the threshold for picky eating and needs specialist multidisciplinary care alongside iron replacement (Source: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry; ANZAED).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Developmentally normal picky eating; provide parental reassurance and dietitian food-chaining advice
options.rationale: Two-centile weight-crossing and iron-deficient anaemia move this out of normal picky-eating variance into a disorder requiring specialist assessment (Source: ANZAED).

options.text: Atypical anorexia nervosa; commence family-based treatment focused on weight restoration
options.rationale: Anorexia (typical or atypical) requires body-image disturbance or fear of weight gain, which is explicitly absent here (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Rumination disorder; refer for behavioural intervention to reduce regurgitation
options.rationale: Rumination disorder requires repeated regurgitation of food, which is not described; the gagging on new foods is sensory-based avoidance, not rumination (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Coeliac disease-driven food refusal; commence gluten-free diet empirically and repeat bloods in six weeks
options.rationale: Empirical gluten-free diet before coeliac serology invalidates future testing; food selectivity is sensory-driven rather than symptom-driven (Source: GESA).

explanation.summary: ARFID is distinguished from picky eating by weight loss or faltering growth, nutritional deficiency, dependence on supplements or psychosocial impairment - without body-image disturbance.
key_points: ARFID subtypes: sensory-based avoidance, lack of interest in eating, fear of aversive consequences
Two-centile weight-crossing is a specialist-referral threshold
Iron and B12 are the commonest deficiencies at diagnosis
Coeliac serology BEFORE any gluten-free trial
explanation.pearls: ARFID is not a rare diagnosis; it is often mislabelled as picky eating for years before growth failure prompts specialist input.

sources.label: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

subtopic_detail: Adolescent depression - SSRI choice and activation monitoring
stem:
A 14-year-old girl with moderate major depressive disorder has completed 10 sessions of cognitive behavioural therapy through headspace without symptomatic improvement. She continues to describe pervasive low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep, and impaired school engagement. She has intermittent passive suicidal ideation without plan or intent. She lives with both parents who are engaged and willing to attend follow-up.

You are the child and adolescent psychiatry registrar. You have discussed adding pharmacotherapy with the young person and her parents, and all agree to proceed. She has no personal or family history of bipolar disorder, no cardiac history, and takes no medications.

Her father asks how you will keep her safe in the first weeks of treatment.

data_table.Risk: Passive suicidal ideation, no plan or intent

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate pharmacological choice and monitoring plan?

options.text: Fluoxetine 10 mg daily with weekly face-to-face review for the first four weeks
options.rationale: Fluoxetine is the only SSRI with a positive risk-benefit profile in adolescent major depressive disorder in AU and international guidance and is first-line when medication is added. The TGA and equivalent regulators require enhanced monitoring in the first four weeks because activation and paradoxical worsening of suicidal ideation are more common in adolescents than adults; face-to-face review weekly during that window is standard (Source: headspace clinical practice guidelines; Australian Medicines Handbook; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg daily with fortnightly review from week two
options.rationale: Sertraline is not first-line in AU adolescent MDD; fortnightly review from week two also misses the peak activation window (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Venlafaxine 37.5 mg daily with monthly review
options.rationale: Venlafaxine has an unfavourable risk-benefit profile in adolescents (increased suicidality signal, discontinuation reactions) and is not first-line (Source: AMH).

options.text: Mirtazapine 15 mg nocte with review at six weeks for response
options.rationale: Mirtazapine is not first-line in adolescent MDD and six-week review misses early activation and adverse-effect monitoring (Source: AMH).

options.text: Amitriptyline 25 mg nocte with monthly review
options.rationale: Tricyclic antidepressants have no demonstrated efficacy in paediatric depression and are cardiotoxic in overdose - contraindicated first-line for adolescent MDD (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Fluoxetine is first-line in adolescent major depressive disorder after inadequate psychological therapy response; weekly face-to-face review is required in the first four weeks for activation and suicidality monitoring.
key_points: Fluoxetine is the only SSRI with net-positive adolescent RCT evidence
Enhanced monitoring: weekly review for 4 weeks then fortnightly to week 12
Screen for family history of bipolar before starting any antidepressant
Combined SSRI plus CBT outperforms either alone (TADS)
explanation.pearls: Activation in the first two weeks is distinct from emergent suicidality but both need active enquiry.

subtopic_detail: Adolescent bipolar disorder recognition and mood stabiliser choice
stem:
A 17-year-old boy is admitted to an adolescent psychiatric unit with a two-week history of markedly reduced sleep (about 2 hours per night), pressured speech, grandiose plans to "launch three companies", spending his savings on equipment, and a euphoric elevated mood. This is his second such episode. Between episodes he is fully well and functional. His mother has bipolar I disorder and takes lithium.

Six months ago during his first episode he was commenced on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily, tolerated well without weight gain, and has been adherent since. He is medically well with normal renal function, LFTs and thyroid function. He is on no other medication.

He would prefer a medication that will let him continue school-based sport this year.

data_table.Presentation: Second manic episode, euphoric type, sleep 2 h/nt, grandiosity, disinhibited spending
data_table.Bloods: Renal function, LFTs, TFTs within normal limits

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate change in mood-stabiliser strategy for maintenance?

options.text: Transition to lithium with baseline renal, thyroid and parathyroid testing and titration to a target level of 0.6-0.8 mmol/L
options.rationale: A second manic episode on adequately dosed valproate defines maintenance-treatment failure in a young man with a first-degree relative with bipolar I disorder. Lithium remains the best-evidenced maintenance mood stabiliser overall and has a specific efficacy signal in classical euphoric mania with a positive family history - exactly this phenotype. Baseline renal, thyroid and parathyroid function are mandatory, and 0.6-0.8 mmol/L is the standard AU maintenance range (Source: RANZCP; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; AMH).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Increase sodium valproate to 1500 mg daily and continue as monotherapy maintenance
options.rationale: Valproate has failed to prevent a second episode at an adequate dose in a young man; dose escalation risks toxicity without addressing the modality mismatch, and valproate carries teratogenicity considerations if he later fathers a child (Source: AMH).

options.text: Cross-taper to lamotrigine and titrate over six weeks to 200 mg daily
options.rationale: Lamotrigine has strong evidence for bipolar depression prevention but is a poor anti-manic and would not protect against further manic episodes in a manic-predominant phenotype (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Add olanzapine 10 mg nocte as long-term adjunct to valproate
options.rationale: Chronic olanzapine addition in an adolescent carries substantial metabolic burden and would restrict school-based sporting activity via weight gain and sedation; add-on antipsychotic is reserved after mood-stabiliser optimisation (Source: AMH).

options.text: Stop valproate and use fluoxetine long-term for prevention of recurrence
options.rationale: Antidepressant monotherapy is contraindicated in bipolar I disorder because it precipitates mania; this would worsen the illness (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Recurrence of classical euphoric mania on adequately dosed valproate with a first-degree family history of bipolar I disorder is a strong indication to move to lithium maintenance with the standard AU 0.6-0.8 mmol/L target range.
key_points: Lithium is best-evidenced maintenance stabiliser and specifically effective in euphoric family-history-positive phenotypes
Baseline before lithium: U&Es, TFTs, corrected calcium/PTH, ECG, weight, urinary hCG in reproductive-age women
Lamotrigine prevents depressive episodes, not manic
Antidepressant monotherapy is contraindicated in bipolar I
explanation.pearls: Adolescent bipolar recognition is delayed by an average of about a decade; family history should raise the threshold to treat depressive symptoms with SSRI monotherapy.

sources.label: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

subtopic_detail: Ultra-high-risk / early intervention psychosis service referral
stem:
An 18-year-old university student is brought by his older sister to a metropolitan GP. Over four months he has become preoccupied that classmates "know his thoughts" and that background traffic noises "seem to comment on him". These experiences fluctuate, he retains partial insight ("I know it sounds strange"), and they occur several times a week. He has withdrawn socially and dropped from A to D grades.

His paternal uncle has schizophrenia. He denies substance use and a urine drug screen is negative. He has no current suicidal ideation and no violent thoughts. He has never had a definite hallucination or fixed delusion, and no episode has lasted more than a few minutes.

He would like help but is worried about "being put on antipsychotics".

data_table.Symptoms: 4-month attenuated positive symptoms, partial insight, fluctuating

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Refer to a specialist youth early intervention psychosis service for ultra-high-risk assessment and staged psychosocial care
options.rationale: Attenuated psychotic symptoms with functional decline, family history and preserved but faltering reality-testing meet ultra-high-risk (UHR) criteria. AU practice through headspace and EPPIC-model services (e.g. Orygen, EIS) is staged psychosocial care first (CBT-p, family work, functional recovery) with antipsychotic medication reserved for transition to first-episode psychosis or high-risk phenotypes; early referral into a youth-specific service reduces transition rates and treatment delay (Source: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry; headspace and Orygen EPPIC guidance).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Commence olanzapine 5 mg daily and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotic medication is not first-line in UHR because it exposes many young people who would never transition to metabolic and neurological harm; psychosocial intervention comes first (Source: headspace and Orygen EPPIC guidance).

options.text: Reassure that experiences are subclinical and review in three months if worsening
options.rationale: UHR carries a 15-30% one-year transition risk; watchful waiting without specialist input misses the highest-value intervention window (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Detain under state mental health legislation for inpatient assessment
options.rationale: Involuntary detention requires risk to self or others plus mental illness meeting statutory criteria; a cooperative help-seeking young person with no risk features does not meet the threshold (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Commence high-dose fish oil monotherapy without specialist referral and review in six months
options.rationale: Omega-3 has small trial evidence in UHR and may be adjunctive within specialist care, but as standalone GP-managed intervention it misses staged psychosocial care and monitoring (Source: headspace and Orygen EPPIC guidance).

explanation.summary: Attenuated psychotic symptoms with functional decline in a young person meet ultra-high-risk criteria; the AU standard is early referral to a youth EPPIC-model early intervention service for staged psychosocial care.
key_points: UHR triad options: attenuated positive symptoms, brief intermittent psychotic symptoms, or genetic/functional decline
Antipsychotic medication is second-line unless transition or severity
CBT for psychosis and family work are first-line UHR interventions
AU services: EPPIC (Vic), EIS (NSW), headspace early intervention streams
explanation.pearls: Reducing duration of untreated psychosis is one of the strongest predictors of long-term functional outcome.

sources.label: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

stem:
A 15-year-old boy with confirmed ADHD (combined presentation) has completed a psychoeducation and behavioural programme and continues to have significant academic impairment and impulsivity. He is otherwise medically well with no cardiac history and normal blood pressure and heart rate. He has already obtained his learner driver permit and drives with his father to and from a rural school. He plays school rugby and lives in a shared household where a younger sibling has a history of medication ingestion.

You are the paediatric registrar and both the young person and his parents have agreed to commence stimulant medication after a structured discussion of options. The specialist has authority under state schedule 8 regulations to prescribe.

He wants to be able to concentrate throughout the school day and while driving.

data_table.Diagnosis: ADHD combined, moderate to severe functional impairment
data_table.Household: Younger sibling with prior medication ingestion

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial stimulant prescription?

options.text: Long-acting methylphenidate once daily with baseline and 3-monthly BP, HR, weight and height monitoring
options.rationale: Long-acting once-daily stimulant formulations (methylphenidate OROS or dexamphetamine long-acting) are preferred first-line in adolescent ADHD in AU because they avoid a midday school-based dose, provide steadier coverage during driving, and have lower diversion and misuse potential than short-acting immediate-release preparations - particularly relevant here with a younger sibling with prior medication ingestion. Baseline and 3-monthly cardiovascular, weight and height monitoring is standard (Source: RACP ADHD clinical practice points; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; AMH).

options.text: Immediate-release methylphenidate three times daily with weekly blood pressure checks
options.rationale: Short-acting three-times-daily dosing requires a school dose (adherence and diversion concerns), and weekly BP monitoring is more intensive than needed once stable; not preferred first-line in adolescents (Source: RACP).

options.text: Atomoxetine once daily as first-line pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is a reasonable non-stimulant alternative (e.g. substance-use risk, tic disorder, stimulant intolerance) but has smaller effect size and is second-line to stimulants in uncomplicated adolescent ADHD (Source: AMH).

options.text: Clonidine once daily as first-line pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: Clonidine is generally adjunctive (particularly for sleep or tics) and is not first-line monotherapy for adolescent ADHD (Source: AMH).

options.text: Modafinil once daily as first-line pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: Modafinil is not TGA-approved for ADHD and is not recommended first-line in AU adolescent practice (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Long-acting stimulants (methylphenidate or dexamphetamine) are first-line in adolescent ADHD, providing steady coverage across the school day and reducing diversion risk compared with immediate-release preparations.
key_points: Long-acting formulations reduce peer diversion and household ingestion risk
Baseline: cardiac history, BP, HR, weight, height, family history of sudden cardiac death
Ongoing: 3-monthly BP, HR, weight, height
Non-stimulants (atomoxetine, guanfacine) are second-line or where stimulants are contraindicated
explanation.pearls: AU state legislation for schedule 8 stimulant prescribing typically restricts initiation to paediatricians and psychiatrists; GP shared care requires an authorised specialist letter.

subtopic_detail: Late-diagnosis autism spectrum in adolescent girls with masking
stem:
A 14-year-old girl is referred by her GP for a second opinion after a two-year history of school-refusal and increasing anxiety. Trials of SSRI and CBT for generalised anxiety have produced only marginal improvement. Her mother reports she is "a different child at home", where she is exhausted, easily overwhelmed and needs a rigid post-school decompression routine. At school she has a small group of friends, is academically strong, and staff describe her as "quiet but coping".

Her developmental history includes early intense interests (rocks, then horses, currently a K-pop group), long-standing sensory sensitivities to labels, seams and fluorescent light, and difficulty with unstructured social situations. She has never had a formal developmental assessment.

She finds the noise and crowding in secondary school "unbearable but I copy what the popular girls do so no-one notices".

data_table.Home vs school pattern: Marked home dysregulation with school 'holding it together'
data_table.Developmental features: Intense interests, sensory sensitivities, unstructured-social difficulty

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in her assessment?

options.text: Refer for a multidisciplinary autism spectrum disorder assessment using a female-sensitive tool such as the GQ-ASC
options.rationale: Home-school dissociation (holding together at school then collapsing at home), long-standing sensory sensitivities, focused intense interests and social camouflaging in a girl with treatment-refractory anxiety are the flag constellation for missed adolescent autism spectrum disorder in girls. AU practice is a multidisciplinary assessment using tools sensitive to female phenotype masking (e.g. Girls Questionnaire for Autism Spectrum Condition, GQ-ASC) before escalating anxiety pharmacotherapy (Source: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry; NHMRC-endorsed National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorders in Australia).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Spectrum Disorders in Australia

options.text: Increase her SSRI to the maximum adolescent dose and add clonazepam for acute anxiety
options.rationale: Adding a benzodiazepine in an adolescent with treatment-resistant anxiety is not endorsed and skips a critical diagnostic reformulation; the anxiety may be secondary to unrecognised autism (Source: AMH).

options.text: Refer for individual psychodynamic psychotherapy as the anxiety may reflect unconscious conflict
options.rationale: Individual psychodynamic therapy is not first-line for adolescent anxiety and does not address the missed developmental diagnosis being flagged (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Recommend home-schooling for the remainder of the year and review in twelve months
options.rationale: Withdrawing from school without diagnostic clarification removes social scaffolding and is not indicated as a primary intervention (Source: headspace).

options.text: Prescribe risperidone for irritability given her home dysregulation
options.rationale: Risperidone is reserved for severe irritability in a confirmed autism spectrum diagnosis and would not be an appropriate first step before assessment (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Late-diagnosis autism spectrum in adolescent girls typically presents as treatment-refractory anxiety with a home-school dissociation pattern and social camouflaging; multidisciplinary assessment using female-sensitive tools should precede further pharmacotherapy.
key_points: Female phenotype: masking, small friendship groups, intense socially acceptable interests
Home 'meltdown' vs school 'holding together' is a red flag pattern
Sensory sensitivities are often long-standing
AU National Guideline recommends multidisciplinary assessment
explanation.pearls: About half of autistic girls are not diagnosed until adolescence or adulthood; many receive multiple prior anxiety and depression diagnoses.

sources.label: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Spectrum Disorders in Australia

subtopic_detail: Conduct disorder vs ODD - discrimination and family intervention
stem:
A 13-year-old boy is referred by his school after 18 months of escalating behavioural difficulty. He has been repeatedly caught in physical fights, has stolen from classmates and shops, was recently cautioned by police for setting a small fire in a park bin, and left home overnight twice without permission in the past month. He shows limited concern about the impact of these behaviours on others.

At home he lives with his single mother and younger brother. His mother reports she has "lost control". There is no substance use disclosed and no evidence of a mood or psychotic disorder. His school achievement is average.

He is willing to attend appointments with his mother but not alone.

data_table.Behaviour pattern: 18 months of aggression to people, property destruction, theft, serious rule violations
data_table.Home: Single-parent family, mother reports loss of behavioural control
data_table.Comorbidity: No substance use, no mood or psychotic disorder

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate diagnosis and initial intervention pairing?

options.text: Conduct disorder; refer for a manualised parent management training program with adolescent family therapy
options.rationale: Physical aggression to people, property destruction (fire-setting), theft and serious rule violation (overnight absences) meet DSM-5 criteria for conduct disorder rather than oppositional defiant disorder, which is characterised by defiance and irritability without the persistent violation-of-others'-rights pattern. First-line intervention is a manualised family-based program (parent management training such as Parent-Child Interaction Therapy or Triple P Teen) combined with family therapy; medication has no primary role (Source: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry; RCH Melbourne CPG - Behavioural problems).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Oppositional defiant disorder; provide parental reassurance and school liaison only
options.rationale: The pattern involves aggression and serious rule violation, which exceed ODD criteria; underdiagnosing risks under-treatment of a condition with a strong trajectory to antisocial personality disorder if untreated (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Antisocial personality disorder; commence risperidone for aggression management
options.rationale: Personality disorder diagnosis is not made before age 18 in most AU practice; risperidone is not first-line and family intervention has better evidence (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Emerging borderline personality disorder; refer for dialectical behaviour therapy for adolescents
options.rationale: The presentation lacks the emotion dysregulation, self-injury and interpersonal instability of BPD; conduct disorder is the correct formulation and DBT-A is not its evidence-based first-line therapy (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Adolescent onset bipolar disorder; commence lithium after baseline investigations
options.rationale: There is no evidence of mania, hypomania or mood episode; irritability and rule-breaking alone do not meet bipolar criteria (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

explanation.summary: A persistent pattern of aggression to people, property destruction, deceitfulness or theft, and serious rule violations for 12 months or more meets DSM-5 conduct disorder; first-line treatment is manualised parent management training with family therapy.
key_points: ODD: defiance and irritability without violation-of-rights pattern
Conduct disorder specifier 'with limited prosocial emotions' identifies callous-unemotional traits
Manualised programs: PCIT (younger), Triple P Teen, Multisystemic Therapy
Medication is adjunctive, targeting comorbid ADHD or aggression only after psychosocial optimisation
explanation.pearls: Early onset (before age 10) predicts worse long-term outcome; adolescent-onset conduct disorder has a better prognosis with intervention.

sources.label: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

subtopic_detail: Adolescent substance use screening - CRAFFT and MI
stem:
A 16-year-old boy attends his GP for a sports pre-participation review. In the HEEADSSS interview he discloses using cannabis "most weekends" with friends and occasional alcohol at parties. He denies driving under the influence but has been a passenger in a friend's car after his friend had been smoking. He has not tried other substances and is doing reasonably well academically.

He is receptive to discussion but says "I don't think it's really a problem".

He agreed to answer standardised screening questions.

data_table.High-risk exposure: Passenger in car with cannabis-using driver

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial screening and intervention approach?

options.text: Administer the CRAFFT screen and deliver a brief motivational interviewing intervention with follow-up
options.rationale: CRAFFT is the validated adolescent substance use screen recommended in AU primary care and youth mental health settings, with two or more affirmative answers indicating need for brief intervention. Motivational interviewing (open questions, reflections, developing discrepancy, rolling with resistance) is the evidence-based brief intervention style for ambivalent adolescents and outperforms confrontation or advice-giving (Source: headspace clinical practice guidelines; RACGP).

options.text: Administer the AUDIT-C only as it is validated for alcohol screening
options.rationale: AUDIT-C screens alcohol alone and misses cannabis, which is the dominant substance here; CRAFFT covers multiple substances plus driving-related risk (Source: RACGP).

options.text: Provide a written pamphlet on cannabis harms and review in six months
options.rationale: Passive pamphlet-only interventions in ambivalent adolescents have minimal behavioural effect and miss the opportunity for a validated screen and brief MI intervention (Source: headspace).

options.text: Refer directly to a residential drug and alcohol program
options.rationale: Residential treatment is disproportionate to the severity; graded stepped-care starts with brief screening and MI in primary care (Source: headspace).

options.text: Tell his parents so they can supervise him more closely
options.rationale: Unilateral parental disclosure without discussion violates confidentiality unless a safeguarding threshold is met and undermines therapeutic engagement (Source: RACGP).

explanation.summary: CRAFFT is the AU-recommended validated adolescent substance-use screen; brief motivational interviewing is the evidence-based initial intervention for ambivalent users.
key_points: CRAFFT: Car, Relax, Alone, Forget, Family/Friends, Trouble - 2+ suggests brief intervention
MI spirit: partnership, acceptance, compassion, evocation
Confidentiality is default; parental disclosure requires safeguarding trigger
Follow-up is core to brief intervention effect
explanation.pearls: The Car question (been a passenger with an intoxicated driver) is a strong single-item risk marker for adolescent injury.

subtopic_detail: Complex trauma - TF-CBT vs EMDR modality fit
stem:
A 15-year-old girl in kinship foster care presents with a four-year history of intrusive nightmares, hypervigilance, avoidance of school toilet cubicles (where the index abuse occurred), emotion dysregulation, and negative beliefs about self. She has capacity to describe her experiences verbally and, with support, can identify emotions and triggers. She was removed from her birth family at age 11 after chronic physical abuse and neglect.

Her kinship carer is engaged and consistent and willing to attend sessions. She has good rapport with her existing clinician and would prefer a structured skills-based approach over a technique that involves eye movements. She has no active suicidality and is medically well.

data_table.Presentation: PTSD symptoms plus complex-trauma features, 4-year duration
data_table.Carer engagement: Kinship carer consistent and willing to attend

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate trauma-focused psychotherapy to recommend?

options.text: Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy for adolescents with kinship carer involvement
options.rationale: TF-CBT for adolescents (TF-CBT-A) and EMDR both have strong evidence for youth PTSD; the modality choice is driven by developmental fit, carer availability and young-person preference. TF-CBT-A's structured psychoeducation, coping skills, and gradual exposure through the trauma narrative fits this young person's verbal ability, stated preference for a structured skills-based approach, and the presence of an engaged carer who can be involved in conjoint sessions; carer involvement is a core component (Source: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry; Phoenix Australia AU Guidelines for the Treatment of PTSD).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing therapy without carer involvement
options.rationale: EMDR has good evidence but does not match the young person's stated preference against eye-movement techniques, and it does not build in carer involvement that this kinship-care context supports (Source: Phoenix Australia).

options.text: Psychodynamic play therapy weekly for twelve months
options.rationale: Non-directive play therapy is not a first-line trauma-focused therapy for adolescents and lacks the exposure and skills components that address PTSD symptoms (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Prolonged exposure therapy monotherapy with imaginal and in vivo exposure only
options.rationale: Prolonged exposure is manualised for adults and lacks the developmentally graded skills-building phases essential in complex-trauma adolescent care (Source: Phoenix Australia).

options.text: Sertraline monotherapy without trauma-focused psychotherapy
options.rationale: Trauma-focused psychotherapy is first-line for adolescent PTSD; SSRIs are adjunctive and are second-line when psychotherapy is unavailable or has failed (Source: Phoenix Australia).

explanation.summary: Both TF-CBT-A and EMDR are first-line trauma-focused psychotherapies for adolescent PTSD; modality choice is guided by developmental fit, carer involvement, and the young person's preference.
key_points: TF-CBT-A: PRACTICE components (Psychoeducation, Relaxation, Affective modulation, Cognitive coping, Trauma narrative, In vivo exposure, Conjoint parent-child, Enhancing safety)
EMDR: bilateral stimulation with structured 8-phase protocol
Complex trauma in youth benefits from a phase-based approach (safety and skills before narrative)
Medication is adjunctive
explanation.pearls: Carer involvement is a stronger effect-size modifier in adolescent PTSD than the specific choice between TF-CBT-A and EMDR.

sources.label: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

subtopic_detail: School refusal - anxiety-driven presentation and graded return
stem:
A 12-year-old girl has not attended school for six weeks. Each morning she reports abdominal pain, nausea, and reluctance to leave the house; symptoms resolve by mid-morning when she is allowed to stay home. She spends the day quietly on the couch with her mother, does not truant with peers, has no antisocial behaviours, and completes some homework her mother collects. She has recently started year 7 at a large secondary school after a small primary school.

On assessment she is worried her parents will die while she is at school and describes checking her mother's location on a shared phone app frequently. There is no bullying, substance use, mood or psychotic disorder. She would like to "get back to school but not straight away".

Her parents ask what to do next.

data_table.Pattern: Somatic complaints resolving by mid-morning, no truancy, no antisocial features
data_table.Cognitions: Fears of parental harm; reassurance-seeking via phone tracking

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Coordinate a graded return-to-school plan with the school and CBT targeting separation anxiety, involving parents to reduce accommodation behaviours
options.rationale: Anxiety-driven school refusal (staying home with parent, no antisocial features, separation-anxiety cognitions, wants to attend but cannot) is distinguished from conduct-driven truancy (truants with peers, defiance, antisocial behaviours). First-line management is a coordinated graded return-to-school plan with the school, CBT targeting the anxiety, and parental work to reduce accommodation behaviours (e.g. constant reassurance, location-tracking). Prolonged absence without a plan worsens prognosis (Source: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry; headspace clinical practice guidelines).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Support home-schooling for the remainder of the year and re-assess enrolment for year 8
options.rationale: Withdrawing from school reinforces avoidance, worsens long-term anxiety-disorder outcomes, and is not indicated when the young person and family are engaged and treatable (Source: headspace).

options.text: Commence an SSRI as monotherapy and defer return-to-school planning until a treatment response
options.rationale: SSRI has a role in moderate to severe paediatric anxiety, but delaying school return waiting for pharmacological response entrenches avoidance; graded return runs in parallel (Source: headspace).

options.text: Refer to child protection given her non-attendance
options.rationale: Non-attendance driven by anxiety with engaged parents does not meet child-protection thresholds; escalation risks harm to the therapeutic relationship and misuses statutory resources (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Prescribe short-course diazepam each morning to allow her to attend school
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are contraindicated for paediatric anxiety management (dependence, disinhibition, cognitive effects) and do not treat the underlying avoidance (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Anxiety-driven school refusal is managed by a coordinated graded return-to-school plan with CBT targeting the underlying anxiety and parental work to reduce accommodation, not by withdrawing from school or waiting for medication response.
key_points: Anxiety pattern: stays home with parent, no antisocial features, wants to attend
Conduct pattern: truants with peers, defiance, antisocial features
Parental accommodation (reassurance, phone tracking) maintains anxiety
SSRI is adjunctive when moderate to severe or CBT insufficient
explanation.pearls: Every week of school absence beyond four weeks approximately doubles the difficulty of return; early graded re-engagement matters.

sources.label: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
